description: Dem kaiserlich und königlichen Hofbrandrat obliegt die vorschriftsmäßige Auswertung und fachgerechte Harmonisierung von satellitengestützten MODIS- und VIIRS-Telemetriedaten. Gemäß unserem verbindlichen Dienstleitsatz „Ex Alto Contra Ignem“ gewährleisten wir strikt geregelte Dienstabläufe zur lückenlosen Erfüllung der übergeordneten, globalen Brandbekämpfungsdirektive.
summary:
We developed Pyrochrone, a web app that shows how much fire activity there was in any region of the world, month by month, from 2002 until today. It is based on NASA FIRMS satellite hotspots.

The problem is that the fire data comes from two different satellites. Until 2012 there is only MODIS, after that, VIIRS is available, and VIIRS detects around four times more fires because it has a much finer resolution. If you simply put both together, it looks like fires suddenly increased in 2012, which is of course wrong.

To solve this, we trained a machine learning model (LightGBM) on the years when both satellites were flying. It learns how many VIIRS hotspots MODIS would have seen in each place and month. So we can convert the old data to the VIIRS scale and get one consistent time series of more than 20 years.

In the app you select an area on the map and immediately see a fire calendar that shows which months were unusual compared to a normal year. This is important for fire managers, emergency services and scientists, because they can see long-term trends and extreme seasons without working with raw satellite data.
details:
What does it do?

Pyrochrone is a web app that shows fire activity for any place in the world, month by month, from July 2002 until today. We use satellite fire data from NASA FIRMS, hundreds of millions fire detections worldwide.

The user sees a world map with hexagons. The colour shows how many fires there were in the chosen time period. When you zoom in, the hexagons get smaller and you see more details. You can draw a rectangle or a polygon on the map, or type in coordinates. Then the side panel shows information about this area:

- the total number of fires

- the month with the most fires

- the most active year

- a "fire calendar" with one row for every year and one column for every month

The calendar can show the numbers, or compare each month with a normal year. So you can see very fast if a fire season was unusual. For example, in south-east Australia, December 2019 had 37 times more fires than a normal December. There is also a 3D globe that shows the fire seasons month by month. In the full version, users can download the fire data of their area as a CSV file; this is switched off in our public demo.

How does it work?

The biggest problem was combining the data of two different satellites. Until January 2012 we only have data from MODIS. After that we use VIIRS. VIIRS finds about four times more fires, because it can see smaller fires. If you just put both datasets together, it looks like fires suddenly increased in 2012, but this is not true.

Our solution: between 2012 and 2020 both satellites were working at the same time. We use these years to train a machine learning model (LightGBM), which learns how many fires VIIRS would have seen when MODIS saw a certain number of fires. The model uses 18 inputs, for example the number of MODIS fires, their strength, the neighbouring areas, the month and the location. With this model we convert the old MODIS data to the VIIRS level. So we get one consistent time series of more than 20 years. From 20 January 2012 we use the real VIIRS data.

We also separate fires in nature from other heat sources, like factories, gas flares, oil platforms and places that burn all year. They are hidden by default, but users can switch them on. Volcanoes are removed completely.

Benefits and impact

Fire managers, emergency services, scientists and journalists can look at more than 20 years of fire history in a few seconds. They don't need to download and process big satellite files themselves. They can find long-term trends, compare this year's fire season with past years and find unusual months. Because the data of the two satellites is combined correctly, a change in the chart is a real change in fire activity, not just a change of satellite.

Tools and technologies

- Data processing: Python, DuckDB, H3 (hexagon grid system), LightGBM, pandas and Jupyter notebooks

- Backend: FastAPI (Python). The data is prepared in advance.

- Frontend: React and TypeScript, MapLibre and deck.gl for the map, ECharts for the charts, three.js for the 3D globe, and Tailwind CSS

- Hosting: one Docker container on Google Cloud Run. It turns off when nobody is using it. We tested it with up to 300 users at the same time.

- Hardware: only our own laptops

How is it creative?

Most fire tools show only one satellite, or both without any correction. We use machine learning to create one consistent dataset, and we keep the app very simple to use. The fire calendar is an easy way to see more than 20 years of fire seasons in one picture.
